title: Respond to a harassment complaint
summary: How you respond becomes the company's defense. Make it prompt, thorough, documented. Retaliation is separately unlawful, so draw the no-retaliation line on day one (the EEOC's published employer guidance is the reference). Take the complaint seriously without judging or promising outcomes. Put interim measures in place that protect the complainant rather than punish them. Pick an investigator without conflicts; for anything senior, outside counsel or an external HR investigator. Run the investigation properly. Decide proportionately, up to termination, and document the reasoning. Close the loop with the complainant. Then watch for retaliation for months; that is where companies lose. An EEOC charge may still come; the file you built is what answers it. Educational guidance, not legal advice.

parts.title: Take it seriously at receipt: acknowledge, no judgments, no promises — and the no-retaliation line drawn on day one (retaliation is separately unlawful)
Interim measures while you investigate — schedule or reporting-line separation chosen to protect the complainant, never to punish them
Choose the investigator: trained and unconflicted internally, or outside counsel / an external HR investigator for anything senior
Run the investigation: interviews, documents, contemporaneous notes — prompt, thorough, documented
Preserve the file: the complaint, interview notes, decisions and their reasons — the file is the company's defense
Decide and act proportionately — up to termination — with the reasoning documented
Close the loop with the complainant (the outcome, not necessarily the details) — and actively watch for retaliation for months

metadata.trigger: An employee reports harassment: by complaint, by email, or in a conversation that just became one.
metadata.supportReason: The investigation, the proportionate-action judgment, and every conversation in this flow are irreducibly human (and counsel-led where it's senior); an agent can preserve the file and keep the timeline straight.

geoNotes.summary: The ACAS Code of Practice governs grievance handling — a fair procedure (investigation, hearing, appeal) is what tribunals expect, and compensation uplifts of up to 25% apply for unreasonably ignoring the Code.

The AGG gives employees a statutory complaint right (§13) and obliges the employer to act against harassment (§12, up to dismissal of the harasser) — a named complaints body (Beschwerdestelle) is expected in every company.

The Code du travail obliges the employer to prevent and act on harcèlement moral and sexuel; companies of 250+ must designate a référent, the CSE has its own alert rights, and the employer's inaction is itself actionable.

The POSH Act 2013 is statutory machinery, not policy: every workplace with 10+ employees must constitute an Internal Committee, complaints go to the IC, and the inquiry runs on a 90-day clock with annual reporting — the ministry for women and child development administers the regime.

The Código do Trabalho bans harassment outright and companies with seven or more employees must adopt a code of good conduct — investigate promptly and document; complaints can escalate to ACT and assédio carries counter-ordinance fines.

Provincial OHS statutes impose written harassment programs and investigation duties (Ontario's OHSA is the model); federally regulated employers follow the Work Place Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations with trained investigators.

contextNeeded.query: the complaint as received, and who is involved (conflicts decide the investigator)
